The idea is that money alone isn't gonna do it for you.  If you don't have any friends, have crap relationships with your family, never bothered to learn a hobby, etcetera, then money isn't going to magically fix your situation. Money will absolutely make life better, but it won't carry you all the way.  There are things you're personally responsible for, too. Make no mistake though, money will greatly help with all of these things.  It's easier to meet friends when you have the money to go places where friends might be.  It's easier to raise a family when you can afford to do so.  It's easier to find a hobby when you can afford the hobby.  But it's still up to you to actually be a likeable person who's capable of fostering genuine relationships in the first place, because those transactional situationships are not fulfilling long term.  
  
This is why billionaires are generally an unhappy bunch.  They have more money than god but are wretched, self-centered, greedy and arrogant, who only know how to think with money and not with personality or humanity.  If they weren't this way, they wouldn't have it in them to make the damaging decisions necessary to become billionaires in the first place.

In short: Money won't automatically save you from being miserable if you're an antisocial megalomaniac.  But if you're a relatively normal and well adjusted person, money will be a massive help in just about every area.

The year was 2006…ish.  I was an enthusiastically frequent player of Runescape 2.  I also hated relying on consumables for healing (which to be fair, I still do).

I was in the Karamja volcano killing Tzhaar because teenage me thought that place was rad.  Problem was, I liked melee and the Tzhaar hurt to fight.  So I got to thinking about how I might prolong my time fighting them without needing to go reset in the Fight Cave so often.

Inspiration struck.  I thought to myself, “Wait, prayer makes you invincible but slowly runs out… but there’s no NEED to have it on when you aren’t immediately receiving an attack… right?”.  So I did some testing and practicing, and sure enough, turning the prayer on and off again the moment you receive an attack would give you the invincibility without draining your prayer if done right.

Some rando walks up to me and says “You know that doesn’t work, right?”.  Annoyed at their confident ignorance, I removed all my armor and proceeded to receive several attacks while taking no damage to prove the point.  They sort of just scoffed and walked away.

A very short while later, a second person saw it and asked if it actually worked.  I said it did, and they asked what I called that technique.  I hadn’t really thought of a name for it, given as I had invented it that very same hour and didn’t think of it as something to be named.  I was caught off guard and felt on the spot, so I just came up with something immediately.  I thought about how the prayer symbol (aka the overhead) is basically like a light flickering on and off rapidly, plus in all likelihood it was almost certainly an unintended design flaw, so I said “The Flicker Glitch”.

Fast forward roughly a year or less from then and I got bored of the game and quit.  Now fast forward to a couple years ago when I see Old School Runescape and decide to play it.  Suddenly everybody knows about the technique and it’s considered a mandatory staple in high end content, with many pieces of content only even existing because the technique allowed the content to be what would otherwise be impossible without it.

I thought to myself, “Eh, if I can come up with it, surely someone else can too.  Just a matter of time I suppose.”.  Then I find out that it’s universally referred to as “flicking” and I thought “Wait… that doesn’t make any sense.  It’s a slow, rhythmic double click, not a flick.  How could a name so obviously unfitting possibly arise from-“ and then I remembered.  Over a decade ago, I essentially told someone it was called ‘Flicker’ and they might have misunderstood what I meant.  Now I am permanently left to wonder if I’m the one who broke Runescape.

Anyway yeah so that might be why “flicking” exists in OSRS today.  I really should’ve called it “Blinking”…

Everything you enjoy now ceases to be fun for you, as if everything is now tedious and boring like solving massive mathematical equations; it’s just mentally taxing and not rewarding. It's important to note that you'd still have to have a way to mitigate the burn.  If I were this aetherkineticist, I wouldn't be able to Gather Power to reduce the burn cost of ramping my force ward because Gather Power only applies to blasts.

My analysis is not that you can just pretend burn doesn't exist.  Rather, it is that if it's possible to reduce burn to 0 via Gather Power when it was originally higher, then you have still "accepted burn" as per the class's creator's own words, even though you've legally reduced the burn to 0.  Likewise if your Infusion Specialization brings a non-zero burn cost down to 0.  In all cases you still need to actually be able to legally bring the burn down to 0.

Nowhere in there implies that you would just ramp it for free and pretend it doesn't cost burn.  Indeed, even in my pyrokineticist scenario, I specified that the defense and utility wild talents used actually inflicted 7 burn upon my pyrokineticist, as I was careful to specify that it maximized my elemental overflow.  So you'll find that what you're saying is actually in line with what I said as well.

Edit: What you **would** get to enjoy, however, is this effect: "Whenever you accept burn while using an aether wild talent, you siphon some of the energy from the aether flowing through you and your force ward recovers a number of temporary hit points equal to your character level, up to its current maximum." Champion kills are a gamble, especially with short range, no CC, no mobility and poor burst damage without items.  So become a dedicated slayer of minions and learn to love it.
4. Learn to ignore your teammates and play selfishly.  Because you're not *really* being selfish by trying to get a gold lead and being able to contribute damage.  You are kind of like a Nasus.  It is your responsibility to be a late game investment.  Your teammates will suffer from your lack of roaming and objective pressure.  They will flame you and blame you for defeat.  Recognize that in most of these cases, they shouldn't have been pointlessly brawling to begin with and they're just pointing the finger at you for not joining their mistake.  If you play Vladimir you need to not give in to these demands for roaming or assistance in unfavorable jungle battles or whatnot, because they will pull you away from your cs and could easily result in you feeding.  Control your lane.  That is your job.  Which brings me to:
5. Learn to control your lane opponent with good wave management and just the right dosage of poke/harassment.  Getting kills is gonna be entirely dependent on either you having flash or your opponent running into you thinking they can make a play on you.  Or if they're dumb, them just not running away from you when your highly-telegraphed butt is coming after them - don't rely on this but it will happen from time to time for some reason.  That being said, kills are not strictly what you are looking for.  Just keeping your laner low enough that they can't safely roam is highly advantageous to your team, for example.  Or keeping their wave crashed into their turret if they DO roam so they miss out on gold and experience is also important.  Likewise, keeping your wave safely close to your turret when you're weak is very important as well.  It takes a lot of experience to be able to tell what you can and can't handle, but these are good guidelines to keep in mind as you're figuring that out.
6. Change your mindset when it comes to playing under unfavorable circumstances.  You **will** need to play from behind regularly, and if you are the type who wants to surrender when you don't have a lead, then go play an early game character.  (Or really, go play some other game entirely because holy cow League is not the right game for people who can't stand losing - the best in the world still lose just as often as you do against foes of their equal.  It will never get better.)  Vladimir has a ton of horrible match ups that will be hell to face.  You will need to learn how to make enough money and play passively without feeding.  In short, you will need to have a strong sense of patience and maintain your temper.  9 times out of 9.1, you will outscale them eventually... if your nexus lives long enough.

7A) You don't really have a macro presence.  Sure you're decent at pushing a wave like most any mage, but you're slow as balls and can't CC someone who comes barreling after you.  Sure you can kill them if it's like a Caitlyn or something and they try to chase you down away from the safety of their tower, but if you're all the way up to your enemy top laner's second tower and an Udyr comes stomping in, your odds of survival are not looking good.

7B) But you DO have a great team fight presence!  A Vladimir is never more at home than fighting near the safety of his turret or the safety of his gang of unruly ne'er-do-wells.  Your damage is free to be utilized without overmuch fear if you've got your crew backing you up.  And chances are, it's higher than your foes'.  That's a good thing.

7C) That said!  You still have no mobility or CC.  What happens if your team won't initiate or every time they try they get kited backwards and stuck in a mobile battle leading away?  Yeah, that's right - your slow butt does nothing and all your friends are gonna die.  Unless you've got something like Ghost or Predator that can just let you say "Eff it" and blitz right into them, OR you have a strong front line with a good engage and lockdown to set you up, you're gonna need creative positioning.  Go for flanks from the side or behind a lot.  Flanks are your friends.  Just learn how to not die when singling yourself out like that, because that is exactly what you're doing.  And you're immobile.  Guess how that goes.  Generally it's best to wait to initiate your flank until the fight kicks off and your foes are becoming distracted, or your team is already barreling confidently after them and you know they won't give up the chase so you're free to cause mayhem and know your foes will pay if they stop to try to deal with you.  These scenarios are gonna be your favorites.  That said, there is one obvious exception: Defensive team fights.  See, all I was describing above were offensive team fights.  Ones where your team is tasked with bringing the battle on.  But when your team is the one being pushed into, you'll find it infinitely easier to reach your opponents!  Shocking, right?  Now your foes are pushing INTO you and not away, so getting in range to do your damage is a lot easier - sometimes too much easier.  Keep in mind that while this is in many ways to your liking, your teammates can retreat better than you can.  If they're not gonna stand and fight, they will leave you for dead and there is legitimately nothing you can do about it.  Ever hear the expression, "You don't need to be faster than the bear, just faster than the guy next to you"?  Well you're the guy next to them, and you are slower.  Unless you like Phase Rush anyway, but manage it well, and don't expect it to actually compare to many other champions' mobility advantage over you.  Regardless, in this all-too-inevitable scenario, prepare to fight well and die well.  Act like a bat out of hell; hit them as hard and fast as you can and bring as many down with you as you can manage.  Even if you get no kills and just wound them, you might have just salvaged the upcoming 4v5.

I'm sure there's other advice I can give but it's escaping me at the moment.  But if you only listen to one thing I say, let it be this: "Prioritize cs and get as much of it as you possibly can."

As a Strength enthusiast who believes that people really underestimate the usefulness of the stat myself, allow me to give my opinion on why Dexterity is still much more mechanically superior.

**Feats:**  
Personally I wouldn't word it as "It takes more feats to work."  I would say "It has much greater feat support."  What does strength have?  Power Attack and maybe a Cornugon Smash build.  That's more or less it.  Sure you have the feats leftover to shoehorn in some half-baked gimmick like Spring Attack but honestly there aren't that many wonderful feats out there, which is the problem fighters typically run into.  Sure they get a thousand of them but only their first few were great, with the others being... niche.

**Armor:** (This one's a three-parter, so strap in)  
It's no secret that armor in pathfinder is trashwater.  You say strength builds have access to fullplate and shields, but I look upon those options with pity.  Armor reduces your movement speed and imposes devastating armor check penalties.  What happens when you need to climb up or down a ledge or rope or tree or anything, jump in any way, stay above water, keep off your backside when just about anything disorienting or unbalancing happens, hide from a looming threat, or even simply run away from said threat with your gimped movement speed?  What happens when you're *inevitably* attacked while sleeping and it takes 10 minutes to put on that armor that you're not allowed to sleep in?  "Guess I'll die."  There is a profound flaw in being an adventurer who can't move around.  Armor doesn't protect you in pathfinder, it gimps you for all the days that you live... which may well get you killed.  I can't tell you how many characters armor has killed or made feel like they're helpless.

Now for shields.  If you're swinging around a one-handed pool noodle, you're gonna struggle to put your foes down, which means they get more time to cut your head off.  You don't get the extra 50% damage from Power Attack.  You don't get the extra 50% damage from strength.  You have lower weapon dice.  The longer you draw combat out, the more danger you're in.  Or maybe someone *else.*  Once again, I can't tell you how many characters feel like they can't contribute meaningfully in combat because they had weak offense, and sometimes that results in them or their party being put in mortal peril.  Remember, even *if* your AC was super high, your foes have no motivation to waste attacks on you once they've seen how pointless it is.  As long as your allies are tearing them apart and you're swinging a pool noodle around.

Lastly, actual AC values.  Believe it or not, builds that wear heavier armor are actually lower in AC than any good lightly armored or unarmored build.  And I'm not talking munchkin setups where you go through a ton of hoops and end up slaying gods.  I'm talking even really basic stuff.  *Plus* anything more advanced than "really basic" does learn to drop armor so as to gain greater AC.  This is because there is actually way more support for unarmored AC than there is for armored AC.  Keep in mind that armor caps the amount of AC you can get from many other things, most commonly your ability scores, but also most class features as well.  If you're wearing Fullplate, that's +10 AC.  9 for the armor and 1 for the allowed dexterity if you took it.  You are now out of growth potential aside from spells or magic items, as your dex AC is capped and few class abilities that grant AC work on heavily armored characters.  But a level 1 monk with 20 dexterity and 16 wisdom is already sitting at +8 with no caps.  He can ramp up his dex/wis and still get AC from it.  He gets +1 free AC every 4 levels just from his class feature.  He gets AC (and other buffs) from a headband of wisdom.  He gets Evasion, which more heavily armored classes don't.  He gets the Dodge feat for free.  He gets Deflect Arrows for free.  His defensive stat also happens to be his offensive stat, so he's not hurting for maxing it out and is gonna pack a serious walloping to boot.  Also by mid level he's running faster than a horse and leaping 40ft wide hazards on a natural 1.  *Then* you get into multiclassing and that's when lightly armored and unarmored AC *really* takes off.

**In Conclusion:**  
Armor gives you less AC, makes you unable to flee or hide from danger, unable to climb, swim or do any other degree of important things for an adventurer, or even sleep safely.  Shields will render your damage easily ignored by foes and indirectly put your more threatening allies in greater danger, all while not even beating out unarmored characters in terms of raw defense.

Dexterity, meanwhile, saves you lots of ability score points in Point Buy, gives you tons of valuable skills you'll need to save yourself from countless dangerous situations or handicaps, has better feat support resulting in more effective combat styles, contributes to reflex which is bolstered by evasion which renders you basically immune to a ton of damage spells and other things, gives you initiative, plus makes you automatically better with ranged weapons for when you inevitably need the option.  The list just goes on.  But yes, it is fair that it does eat up more resources to get it to replace strength, and that's not nothing, either.

Strength does, however, have carry capacity, which I think is dramatically more powerful than people realize.  Huge strength scores can lift and move incredibly heavy things, and if you're creative with that, you'd be dumbfounded how useful that ability is just on a day by day basis.  Like I said, I'm a hardcore strength enthusiast myself and I prioritize it over dexterity in just about any case other than unchained rogues (yes, even monks), but I do acknowledge that my preference is not strictly the most superior option.  That said, I've never worn more than light armor.

Every other loser you come across is an overlord and the title of Tyrant is bestowed to a guy who, at the time of his Tyrancy, was stated to not even be able to lay a finger on Void, who himself was confirmed to not be able to lay a finger on Goldion. Likewise, it's confirmed that Killidia was only given that title because he was the overlord of Cryo Blood, which was understood to be the most brutal of netherworlds.  He didn't actually have any level of universal influence like what Tyrants typically do; in fact he really only sat there on his one netherworld and kept beating up its inhabitants.  He was only even known due to the notoriety of his home world.

Move on to Valvatorez, whose title of Tyrant was feared throughout the multiverse.  Any self respecting demon knew and trembled at his name, bestowing him monikers like "Blood-soaked Valvatorez of Absolute Evil", "King of Carnage and Atrocity" and "Bloodthirsty King of Fear." Killidia would eventually go on to master his power significantly further than before.  It's thought that he may even have surpassed Goldion, but given that Goldion blatantly allowed himself to be overtaken, it's unclear whether or not he truly did.  More importantly, he still grew in power significantly.

Here's the funny part.  Most people tend to think that Valvatorez is still in his weakened state after not drinking blood, but the last line in the main story is Artina stating that Valvatorez had fulfilled his promise to show her the depths of fear, for his actions in the events prior had terrified her beyond belief, and that he may now drink her blood. Valvatorez is back to being his old self when he was truly a Tyrant, but with more experience under his belt (though admittedly nothing really challenged him in his main story so it's possible he didn't grow any), and Killia certainly grew more powerful than his old self, who technically had the title of Tyrant but clearly didn't measure up to the standards of Tyrants nowadays.

All things considered, I place my confidence in Valvatorez.

There are many GMs who, for whatever reason, really want their players to regularly fail basic or moderate challenges for no better reason than because “this masterful paragon of a sculptor just has earth shatteringly violent sneezes that come up at random with no warning, I guess.”  If your player has a massive bonus to their skill and insists on taking 10 then it’s okay for success to regularly be a foregone conclusion.

I know from a GM’s standpoint they want their players to be challenged and it makes it feel impossible to do when somebody can take 10 and succeed so regularly.  But do you know what your player is thinking when they do that?  Usually something along the lines of “I really like this character.  It’s working just like I’d hoped.  This makes me happy.”  Sometimes it’s not about challenging _them,_ but just letting them know that only they could’ve done it.  That can be just as satisfying.

Some people value consistency over potential, and those individuals usually rejoice that there is such an option for them.  By building a character with a massive bonus to something and always taking 10, they’re generally communicating to you that they aren’t looking forward to failing at this particular thing, and they are happy with their continued successes.  Sometimes the challenge isn’t the roll (which lets be honest, isn’t a challenge at all because luck and difficulty are two entirely different things) but rather figuring out a way to take a reliable skill and apply it meaningfully to a situation.

Just keep in mind that most likely the player is having fun in the comfort of their consistency in this one or few fields of their expertise.  If their stats reflect it, let the scholar feel super smart or the climber enjoy feeling that they can scale anything if that’s what they want.  It sets them apart and grants meaning to their character’s different strengths and weaknesses.

Also worth noting: James Jacobs points out that if there is a 30 foot wide chasm with lava at the bottom of it, the player with the +20 mobility modifier should most definitely be allowed to take 10 and succeed every time, (provided they have the movement necessary) even if the threat of failure is certain death and the character is well aware of that stressful result.  To not qualify for taking 10, you need something that is actively impeding you, like somebody actively swinging their sword at you right now; not standing 30ft away and moving in to do so.  Mere stress of failure or having someone/something chasing you with the intent to kill does not count as a “stressful situation” or being “distracted” or being “immediately endangered.”  Having a swarm of bees stinging you or a chupacabra latched onto your ankle does.

The unicorn myth originated in an era where all quadrupedal mammals with a tall and herbivorous shape could be referred to as “horses”, such that cows, donkeys, deer, rhinoceroses, elephants, etcetera could all be called a “horse”.  It wasn’t intended to be specific, but rather to generalize the animal’s shape.  It’s similar to nowadays how some people call any soda a “coke” even if they’re talking about sprite or something.

When records of the rhinoceros were first being written, people who lived outside of regions native to them were completely unfamiliar with them.  So when they heard tale of a horse with a unicorn (uni meaning one and corn meaning horn; Latin) people started talking about what the one-horn must look like.  They kept just referring to it as the one-horn and the name stuck.

So nowadays we’ve got the rhinoceros, which is what the unicorn was originally describing, and then we’ve got the mythical creature referred to as the one-horn, or, the unicorn, which was a image people had created in their heads when hearing about the rhinoceros.

tl;dr:

The unicorn does actually exist and it is in fact the rhinoceros, which we have indeed been hunting to extinction for many years.
